newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Bank of England sees less need for rate rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bank of England sees less need for rate rise.

text.p: Weaker British economic data and the continued strength of sterling have made the need for an interest rise less urgent than was thought in December, Bank of England Governor Eddie George said on Monday.
He told parliament's key Treasury Select Committee it was possible that the soaring pound could push inflation down to the government's 2.5 percent target in the months ahead.

At his December monetary meeting with Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, George said the lack of an immediate quarter-point interest rate rise would probably necessitate a half-point increase early in 1997.

"Two things have happened since then. The exchange rate has gone further and the acceleration in the (economic) data that was apparent in October and November has not persisted. That makes it absolutely less pressing than it was," George said.

The pound has leapt by about 16 percent, measured against a basket of currencies, since August last year. On the statistics front, retail sales tumbled by 0.8 percent in December, casting doubt on the idea that a high street boom was under way.
A stronger pound cuts import prices and therefore eases inflationary pressure. At the same time it hurts exporters as their prices rise.

In its quarterly inflation report released last week, the central bank called for a moderate tightening of monetary policy to increase the chances that underlying inflation, excluding home loan payments, would fall to 2.5 percent.

Many economists said that signalled that the bank was backing off its hawkish line on rates. But George told the committee there had been little or no softening of the bank's stance. "If there has been a softening, it has been pretty small," he said.

George said the bank's forecasts were not the product of an exact science. "It is not inconceivable over the next few months that the strength of sterling comes through more rapidly into retail prices and that actually at the end of parliament...we could indeed be at 2.5 percent."
He conceded that there were already signs that the currency shift was filtering through to retail price inflation.
But he was not convinced that sterling was a "one-way" bet for foreign exchange dealers, climbing endlessly higher.
"If sterling were to join (European) monetary union, I would be very surprised if it were at anything like this level in the exchange rate," he said, to emphasise the point.
The pound, trading at about 2.75 marks late on Monday, dropped as low as 2.17 marks late in 1995, having plunged out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) in September 1992.
Since that low, sterling has clawed back nearly all of the ground it lost. It was by crashing below the key level of 2.7780 marks that the British currency fell out of the ERM.
Despite the pound's recovery, George said a single European currency offered a host of potential pitfalls for Britain with "a beauty and the beast scenario".
"The beauty is the fixed exchange rate but the potential tension (caused by one monetary policy for a number of economies) is what I've called the beast," George told the parliamentary committee.

Noting a difference of three percentage points between British base rates and the German discount rate, six percent versus three percent, he said: "You can have quite a sharp divergence of cyclical positions (between different countries). That's the problem with a one size fits all interest rate.
"That's an example for the sort of tensions that could arise if you moved prematurely to monetary union."
